strengths: Insightful and original observation: The paper identifies that self-attention maps in diffusion models briefly exhibit sharp instance-level boundaries during early denoising/inversion (the Instance Emergence Point, IEP), contrasting with standard vision transformers (e.g., DINO) that primarily group semantically.

Well-motivated and efficient pipeline: The framework carefully designs non-parametric edge extraction (ABDiv via KL divergence) and a one-step self-distillation strategy that eliminates the expensive per-image diffusion forward process at inference time, achieving an 81x speedup (down to 45 ms per image).

Compelling empirical improvements: Evaluated extensively across unsupervised instance segmentation (UIS) and weakly-supervised panoptic segmentation (WPS) across 7 benchmarks (COCO, VOC, LVIS, KITTI, SA-1B, etc.). Notably, tag-supervised segmentation with TRACE outperforms point-supervised baselines without requiring point/box annotations.

Comprehensive ablations and analysis: The paper provides in-depth investigations into divergence metrics (KL vs. JSD/L1/L2), stride lengths, optimal timesteps across multiple architectures (SD1.5, SDXL, SD3.5-L), and comparisons against conventional edge detectors.
weaknesses: High training overhead for distillation: While inference is lightweight and single-pass, generating pseudo-edges and fine-tuning the diffusion backbone with LoRA on ImageNet takes 8–10 days on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, which presents a non-trivial computational footprint.

Heuristic thresholding for pseudo-edges: The construction of ternary edge maps relies on fixed mean and standard deviation offsets (mu +/- sigma) of ABDiv scores. A discussion on how sensitive the downstream segmentation is to these statistical thresholds in challenging scenes (e.g., cluttered textures, thin objects) is relatively limited.

Analysis of failure cases: Although extensive qualitative successes are shown in the appendix, the paper would benefit from a dedicated analysis of failure modes (e.g., highly occluded objects, transparent objects, or instances with very low visual contrast).

strengths: Insightful core discovery: The paper uncovers that self-attention maps in text-to-image diffusion models exhibit a distinct transition window—termed the Instance Emergence Point (IEP)—where self-attention strongly highlights object boundaries, distinct from discriminative ViTs (e.g., DINOv2) and MLLMs which tend to focus on semantic groupings.

Principled and practical extraction pipeline: Attention Boundary Divergence (ABDiv) effectively converts spatial attention divergence into instance boundary cues. The subsequent one-step self-distillation into a lightweight edge decoder neatly solves the per-image inversion bottleneck, achieving an ~81x inference speedup (45 ms vs. 3.7 s).

Strong empirical gains: When used to refine unsupervised instance segmentation baselines (MaskCut, ProMerge), TRACE achieves noticeable improvements (+3.6 to +5.3 APmk on COCO and VOC; validated across 7 datasets in Table 8). In weakly-supervised panoptic segmentation, combining TRACE with tag-supervised methods enables them to surpass point-supervised baselines without requiring instance-level coordinates.

Thorough ablation and comparative analysis: The authors rigorously analyze divergence metrics (KL vs. JSD/L1/L2), diffusion vs. non-diffusion backbones (including large vision models like EVA02 and LLaVA-13B), and standard low-level edge detectors (Canny, HED, PiDiNet, DiffusionEdge).
weaknesses: Computational requirements and backbone scale: The highest-performing configuration relies on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large (8.1B parameters), and distillation on ImageNet requires 8 to 10 days on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. While effective, the heavy model footprint contrasts with traditional unsupervised segmentation baselines built on lightweight backbones.

Reliance on initial mask proposals: TRACE functions primarily as a boundary refiner / separator via Boundary-Guided Propagation (BGP) rather than a standalone end-to-end instance segmenter. Its performance depends inherently on the quality and recall of the upstream segmentation baseline (e.g., MaskCut, ProMerge, or DHR).

Heuristic thresholding in pseudo-label creation: The ternary pseudo-edge map generation relies on mean and standard deviation thresholds ($\mu \pm \sigma$), and mask merging depends on a fixed IoU threshold ($\tau_{BGP} = 0.5$). A deeper sensitivity analysis across varying object densities and scales would strengthen confidence in its generalizability.

Cross-domain transferability of distilled edge decoder: While demonstrated on standard natural image benchmarks (COCO, VOC, KITTI, SA-1B), the paper does not systematically evaluate how well the ImageNet-distilled one-step edge decoder generalizes to atypical domains (e.g., microscopy or aerial imagery) without re-distillation.

strengths: Compelling core insight: The observation that text-to-image diffusion self-attention exhibits an 'Instance Emergence Point' (IEP) where instance-level boundaries transiently appear—unlike discriminative backbones (DINO, CLIP, MLLMs) that primarily model cross-image semantic similarity—is insightful and well-supported.

Well-motivated and efficient pipeline: The combination of IEP identification via KL divergence, non-parametric boundary extraction via Attention Boundary Divergence (ABDiv), and subsequent one-step self-distillation with an edge decoder effectively addresses the computational bottleneck of multi-step diffusion feature extraction (achieving an ~81x speedup, down to ~45 ms per image).

Strong and consistent empirical improvements: TRACE delivers substantial gains across unsupervised instance segmentation (e.g., +4.4 to +5.1 AP on COCO and VOC) and enables tag-supervised panoptic segmentation to surpass point-supervised baselines (e.g., +1.7 to +7.1 PQ). The extensive evaluation across seven distinct benchmarks (COCO, VOC, LVIS, KITTI, Objects365, SA-1B) demonstrates robust generalization.

Comprehensive experimental analysis and ablations: The authors provide thoughtful comparisons against traditional and learned edge detectors (Canny, HED, PiDiNet, DiffusionEdge), proving that low-level texture/intensity contours cannot replace instance-level boundaries. Ablations on divergence metrics (KL vs. JSD/L2/L1) and diffusion vs. non-diffusion backbones clearly validate architectural and algorithmic choices.
weaknesses: Substantial training overhead for distillation: Although test-time inference is fast (one-step forward pass), the distillation stage requires 8 to 10 days of training on ImageNet using an A100 GPU, meaning TRACE is not an entirely off-the-shelf, zero-training plug-in unless the distilled checkpoints are provided.

Computational requirements and backbone scale dependency: The strongest results require large models such as SD3.5-Large (8.1B parameters, 32 GB VRAM). While SD1.5 remains competitive (6.8 APmk vs. 8.2 APmk on COCO 2014), the method's full potential is somewhat tied to high compute and memory capacity.

Reliance on post-processing heuristics: The downstream integration depends on Boundary-Guided Propagation (BGP) and connected component labeling with fixed thresholding (e.g., merging threshold τ_BGP = 0.5). A deeper sensitivity analysis on how BGP handles complex occlusions, overlapping instances of identical color, or very small objects would strengthen the work.

Minor terminology inconsistency: In Section 3.5, the propagation module is introduced as 'Background-Guided Propagation (BGP)', whereas Figure 6 and Appendix D.6 refer to it as 'Boundary-Guided Propagation'. This should be made consistent across the manuscript.

strengths: Compelling conceptual insight: The paper convincingly demonstrates that diffusion model self-attention captures instance-level boundaries early in the denoising trajectory, unlike standard discriminative vision transformers (e.g., DINOv2) or MLLMs which tend to merge adjacent instances of the same category.

Principled formulation: The proposed Instance Emergence Point (IEP) based on inter-step KL divergence is well-motivated and supported by an elegant information-theoretic analysis linking it to maximal Fisher information with respect to noise level.

Practical distillation framework: Formulating Attention Boundary Divergence (ABDiv) with uncertainty masking and distilling it into a lightweight one-step edge decoder at t=0 effectively overcomes the heavy computational overhead of multi-step diffusion inversion, slashing per-image latency from ~3.7s to 45ms.

Comprehensive and rigorous experiments: The method is validated across unsupervised instance segmentation (UIS), weakly-supervised panoptic segmentation (WPS), open-vocabulary segmentation, and direct instance boundary detection on COCO, consistently outperforming strong baselines (including point-supervised methods using only tag supervision).

Thorough ablations and honest discussion of limitations: The authors provide detailed ablations on similarity metrics, decoder architectures, and backbone capacities (SD1.5 to FLUX.1), while transparently detailing failure modes on tiny instances (satellite images) and out-of-distribution domains (histopathology).
weaknesses: Pre-distillation training footprint: While test-time inference is lightweight (45 ms), distilling the instance edge predictor requires 8-10 GPU days on an NVIDIA A100 per diffusion backbone on ImageNet, which is a noticeable training resource requirement.

Reliance on multi-stage post-processing (BGP): Downstream integration relies on Background-Guided Propagation (random-walk affinity propagation and connected component labeling) to separate and merge masks, adding algorithmic complexity on top of raw edge detection.

Custom instance edge benchmark: The direct edge evaluation is benchmarked on a newly synthesized ground-truth edge set derived from COCO panoptic masks; while this makes sense for instance boundaries, evaluation on established edge/boundary datasets or comparison with other high-level edge detectors would further contextualize raw boundary quality.

strengths: Insightful and original core idea: The discovery of the Instance Emergence Point (IEP)—identifying the precise denoising step where self-attention transitions into instance-aware structure via maximal temporal KL divergence—is conceptually neat, well-motivated, and supported by information-theoretic analysis.

Practical and well-engineered pipeline: The paper addresses the severe latency drawback typical of diffusion-based vision approaches by distilling the multi-step IEP and ABDiv signals into a lightweight one-step edge decoder via LoRA, yielding an ~81x inference speedup (45 ms vs. 3682 ms) while improving edge continuity.

Strong empirical performance across multiple setups: Demonstrates substantial improvements in unsupervised instance segmentation (+4.4 to +5.1 AP on COCO/VOC baselines like MaskCut and ProMerge) and weakly-supervised panoptic segmentation, where tag-only supervision with TRACE surpasses point-supervised baselines (e.g., Point2Mask, EPLD).

Extensive comparisons and foundation model analysis: Thoroughly benchmarks 5 diffusion models against 5 non-diffusion vision and multimodal backbones (including DINOv2, EVA-02, and Qwen2.5-VL), clearly illustrating that instance boundary emergence is an intrinsic generative property rather than just an artifact of model scale.

Transparent and thorough analysis of limitations: The authors explicitly evaluate and analyze failure modes on out-of-distribution domains (e.g., histopathology cell segmentation) and tiny objects in satellite imagery (constrained by VAE downsampling).
weaknesses: Distillation requires significant training overhead: While the initial discovery process is training-free, the practical single-step model requires 8–10 GPU days of LoRA fine-tuning on ImageNet on an A100 GPU, which somewhat blurs the line between a purely annotation-free / training-free heuristic and a learned edge detector.

Dependency on post-processing heuristics: The overall segmentation pipeline still relies on Background-Guided Propagation (BGP), connected component labeling, and an IoU-based merge threshold (tau_BGP = 0.5) to assemble masks from edges, introducing algorithmic complexity downstream.

Evaluation on established boundary benchmarks: Edge quality is evaluated on boundaries derived from COCO panoptic masks (which is suitable for instance edges), but comparing against standard boundary benchmarks with semantic/instance annotations (such as Cityscapes semantic boundaries or SBD) would further validate boundary precision against specialized boundary detection literature.

strengths: Novel and insightful observation: The paper identifies the Instance Emergence Point (IEP) where diffusion self-attention transitions from noise to instance-level structure before settling into semantic content, offering a compelling explanation for why diffusion models capture instance boundaries better than discriminative vision transformers.

Principled formulation and theoretical grounding: The proposed Attention Boundary Divergence (ABDiv) and IEP selection criteria are well-formulated, with an informative theoretical justification linking the inter-step KL divergence peak to the maximum Fisher information along the diffusion trajectory.

Practical efficiency via self-distillation: The authors address the severe latency bottleneck of multi-step diffusion inversion by distilling the boundary cues into a lightweight one-step edge decoder at t=0, achieving an 81x speedup (45 ms per image) while preserving boundary connectivity.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The method is validated across unsupervised instance segmentation (UIS), weakly-supervised panoptic segmentation, and open-vocabulary segmentation over numerous benchmarks (COCO, VOC, LVIS, KITTI, Objects365, SA-1B). Crucially, tag-supervised segmentation using TRACE edges outperforms point-supervised baselines.

Thorough ablation and transparent discussion of limitations: The paper evaluates 10 foundation model backbones (diffusion vs. non-diffusion/MLLMs), thoroughly ablates metrics and loss functions, and candidly details failure cases on satellite imagery (due to VAE downsampling) and out-of-distribution histopathology data.
weaknesses: Significant offline distillation overhead: While inference is efficient (45 ms/img), training the one-step edge decoder on ImageNet requires 8–10 GPU days on an NVIDIA A100, which poses a non-trivial computational hurdle for practitioners.

Dependency on post-processing heuristics and base segmenters: TRACE functions primarily as an edge prior and boundary refiner rather than an end-to-end standalone instance segmentation architecture, relying on Background-Guided Propagation (BGP) and heuristic parameters (such as the IoU merge threshold tau_BGP = 0.5) to produce final masks.

Fundamental resolution bottleneck for tiny objects: Because latent diffusion models rely on VAE encoders with spatial downsampling (typically 8x or 16x), TRACE struggles significantly on high-density scenes with very small instances (e.g., satellite imagery, where it degrades baseline performance).

Slightly hyperbolic title phrasing: Framing the generative model as 'secretly an instance edge detector' is somewhat exaggerated, as extracting these edges requires careful timestep identification, cross-neighbor divergence computation, and dedicated distillation.
